blocks.c: Actual pages, torn from a log, in her block capitals, developed over thirty-one years, and she made me copy the whole thing into my own book before she would say another word about it.
WHAT IT TAKES, IN ORDER, AND WHAT IT MEANS:

items: Habits. How you take your coffee. Which way you fold a towel. Free. It takes these to test whether you notice.
Preferences. Songs you liked. Foods. This is the first real charge and it means it has opened an account on you.
Skills. Small ones first. Your handwriting will change. You will lose a language before you lose a knot.
Names. Not people — names. You will remember your sister perfectly and be unable to say what she is called.
Faces. This is where people stop coming back up.

blocks.c: "That's the ladder," she said. "It goes down it in order and it never skips. It's a landlord: it takes rent in the cheapest currency you'll tolerate, and it only escalates when you don't object."

"You write it down and you sign out. That's it. That's the entire defence. A written record with a signature is the only thing it recognises, because a written record with a signature is the only thing it's made of." She tapped my book. "It cannot take what is written down. Not because it's kind. Because a lease is a document, and a document that contradicts itself is void, and it is extremely, extremely afraid of being void."
I wrote all of that down. Then I asked the obvious question.
"Wen. Have you written down everything it's taken from you?"
She did not answer for a while.
"No," she said. "Not for the first four years. I was twenty-four and I thought I'd remember."
